items.title: New York Yankees @ Minnesota Twins: Max Fried vs. Bailey Ober
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
The Yankees are heading to the playoffs. In a season of uncertainty (particularly around injuries), that much is certain after last night’s series-opening comeback victory officially punched their ticket for the ninth time in the last 10 seasons. Everything beyond that, though, is still unknown.

While their playoff spot (and likely the top wild card based on the standings) is secure, the team has made it clear that their aspirations are still to win the AL East, which they trail by 3.5 games with 12 to go. Until they get their hands on the Tampa Bay Rays next week in the Bronx, their playoff journey won’t be set in stone, but games like these are important to ensure that what they do that week can directly control their fate.

Looking to lock up another series win in Minnesota will be Max Fried, who’s probably hoping to go deeper than his last start against Colorado. He labored through 3.1 innings of work and was removed due to pitch count, but should be pretty close to full-go tonight as he continues to build up. Entering play, he has a 2.73 ERA (155 ERA+) and 2.73 FIP across 99 innings in 18 starts. He did not face the Twins in early July at Yankee Stadium, having been on the injured list with the bone bruise in his elbow.

Making the start for Minnesota will be Bailey Ober, who will be toeing the slab for the 23rd time this season. The 31-year-old has been one of their most consistent starters for half a decade now, despite becoming a completely different pitcher as he’s aged. He went from someone who had a very good strikeout rate to one of the lowest among starting pitchers, currently sitting with just 85 strikeouts in 117.2 innings with a 4.28 ERA (98 ERA+). Impressively, he’s only managed to make one career start against the Yankees, allowing three runs in five innings in 2024.

Finesse has always been the way he’s gotten batters out, but it’s particularly true as his fastball velocity and, subsequently, usage have cratered over the years, now sitting at just 88.1 mph on average. He has good command and limits hard contact, but has a big issue with allowing barrels due to middling stuff. Against lefties, it’s changeups and four-seamers with a few sliders mixed in, while he throws them much more evenly against righties alongside a sweeper and sinker.

: Target Field, Minneapolis, MN

: YES, Twins.TV

: WFAN 660/101.9 FM, WADO 1280 (NYY), TIBN, The Wolf 102.9 FM, LosTwins.com (MIN)

: MLB.tv (out-of-market only), Gotham Sports App

For updates, follow us on , , and , and like us on .

items.title: MLB Mid-September Check-in: NL West
items.author: Estevão Maximo
items.content:
Every day, Pinstripe Alley offers updates on what the Yankees’ top American League opponents are up to through the . The AL East is well-trodden ground there, but with the final month of the season just ahead, we’re going to take a peek around MLB as a whole and check in with each of the other five divisions. Who’s surprising? Who’s underwhelming? Who’s simply mediocre at the moment? Read on and find out.

First Place: Los Angeles Dodgers (90-59)

 Max Muncy (4.2 fWAR) Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.3 fWAR)

Perhaps even more clearly than last season, there is a bit of a disconnect between the expectation of how the Dodgers will look come playoff time and their actual record — the latter has been on par with the other two division leaders in the National League for most of the season, not quite lapping the league like the former has been since the offseason. It should be noted that the Dodgers have managed to build a little cushion over Atlanta as of late though, entering the week with a three-game lead in the loss column. It’s understandable how we got here, especially after they made up for the absence of starting pitcher Shohei Ohtani in the playoffs with the addition of Tarik Skubal at the deadline.

Speaking of baseball’s unicorn, the biggest development recently over in Chavez Ravine has been the IL placement of Ohtani with right-biceps inflammation, one of many issues bothering Ohtani for quite a while now. Considering he has already resumed baseball activities, expectations are that he should be back in the lineup come the end of the regular season. The main question is how much these nagging issues will affect Ohtani’s ability to hit in the playoffs — a hobbled-up Ohtani, below his recent standard, still managed to hit 30 homers and accumulate a 142 wRC+ this regular season, both good enough to lead this potent lineup.

Ohtani isn’t the only high-profile hitter currently missing from the Dodgers lineup; they are also without Andy Pages, absent with a fractured hand. That being said, the reigning back-to-back champs are also confident about the return of Pages come playoff time, which would technically leave this lineup at full strength — actual full strength depends on Kyle Tucker’s recent hot stretch carrying over after an incredibly underwhelming first year with the Dodgers. Moving over to the pitching side, the rotation that already dominated last year’s postseason gets the boost of Skubal — once again with both Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell fresh off campaigns in which they seldom pitched in the regular season, combining for just 18 starts.

San Diego Padre

 Fernando Tatis Jr. (4.8 fWAR) Mason Miller (3.5 fWAR)

Potentially the hottest team in the National League right now, the San Diego Padres, as the Yankees recently learned on a trip to Petco Park, possess quite the dangerous team. Since that series with New York, all the Padres have done is win, taking advantage of a soft part of the schedule by sweeping the Nationals and Giants. The NL is so strong that even with this productive run, San Diego is only three games up on Arizona in the loss column for the final Wild Card spot — these two teams are set to play on the final weekend of the season.

The Padres have flourished with the improved form of Fernando Tatis Jr., possessing a 25-14 record since the start of August. Running a lot more than your average team, in large part thanks to the aggressiveness of Tatis — who leads the league having been caught stealing 13 times — the Padres have the rare distinction of possessing three different players with at least 20 stolen bases. Tatis is joined by Jackson Merrill and Xander Bogaerts to make up that dangerous trio on the basepaths.

A key boost to the Padres’ playoff chances comes in the recent return of Nick Pivetta. Just a season ago, Pivetta was outperforming former Yankee Michael King and current AL Cy Young candidate Dylan Cease to be the ace of this staff. It’s a position he more or less slots right back into, although it should be noted that King has kicked things up a notch — and even more importantly, the former Yankee has been healthy the whole year. Overall, this is a sneaky, quality team, and it wouldn’t be a surprise seeing them give any NL division winner a run for their money if they can hold off Arizona.

Third Place: Arizona Diamondbacks (79-71, 11.5 GB)

 Gabriel Moreno (4.4 fWAR) Eduardo Rodríguez (3.2 fWAR)

Guess how many baseball teams currently have not one, not two, but three separate players with an fWAR of 4.0 or higher. That distinction belongs to the Chicago Cubs and the Arizona Diamondbacks. Interestingly, in the middle of the Diamondbacks trio, you won’t find the player who you could argue is Arizona’s most talented hitter, Ketel Marte. After an unexplained absence during a series against the Red Sox that led to him being placed on the Restricted List, Marte has returned to action — while his numbers in September aren’t anything special, his availability dramatically affects the makeup of this lineup.

If you’re wondering how the Diamondbacks got here with a subpar performance from a star hitter and their highest-paid player, Corbin Burnes, basically missing the whole year, it’s been a mix of breakout performances and bounce-back campaigns. Moreno, who had already established himself as a reliable catcher, is producing career-high hitting stats across the board, while Eduardo Rodríguez is having the greatest season of his career by a wide margin in year No. 11 as a big leaguer.

Circling back to Burnes, the former Cy Young winner made his return to the big leagues recently, still on a tight leash. The potential to get Burnes and Marte producing at a high level in the playoffs could make this Arizona team a dangerous one. However, before even thinking about that, they have to run down the Padres, an ungrateful task given how San Diego is playing.

Fourth Place: San Francisco Giants (62-88)

 Rafael Devers (3.4 fWAR)* Logan Webb (3.1 fWAR)

*Technically, Luis Arraez is still in the number one spot at 3.8, but he was traded to the Phillies at the deadline.

After years of unsuccessfully trying to lure a superstar to the Bay Area, the Giants found their man in Rafael Devers. Leaving aside the positive impact of this move for the Yankees, particularly given what Boston took to get rid of him, one player alone has a very limited impact on the fate of a team.

Sure, there are many specific flaws we could point to as to why this team is so close to the bottom, but there are too many to go through them all. Ultimately, it’d be shortsighted to focus on the down year from Logan Webb, for instance, or other specific letdowns for a team whose process seems to be in question.

No matter how you look at it, the reviews around Tony Vitello’s first year as a manager in the big leagues are far from flattering. To call bringing in a skipper without any big-league experience a risky move is an understatement. It’s fair to say that the Buster Posey regime is already under heavy scrutiny.

Last Place: Colorado Rockies (55-94)

 Jake McCarthy (2.8 fWAR) Kyle Freeland (1.1 fWAR)

Something that Mike Tomlin said on a broadcast during Week 1 of the NFL season, quoting a former player, noting that “the Browns is the Browns,” stuck in the back of my mind. That could easily apply to the Colorado Rockies in Major League Baseball, a franchise that has been at the bottom of the barrel for too long to be genuinely optimistic about a rebuild project — at least before seeing promising signs to back that up.

It’s 2026, and Kyle Freeland is still showing up as their most productive pitcher. The injury to Chase Dollander, who has been a rare, exciting young arm to take the mound at Coors Field, certainly hurt this team’s outlook in 2026. But their primary problems remain the same, and a solution doesn’t seem to be on the horizon.

items.title: MLB Mid-September Check-in: NL Central
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
Every day, Pinstripe Alley offers updates on what the Yankees’ top American League opponents are up to through the . The AL East is well-trodden ground there, but with the Trade Deadline behind us, we’re going to take a peek around MLB as a whole and check in with each of the other five divisions. Who’s surprising? Who’s underwhelming? Who’s simply mediocre at the moment? Read on and find out.

We’ve reached the halfway point of September, several teams have now clinched postseason spots, and several more will soon. With just a couple weeks of regular season baseball left, let’s check in on the NL Central.

Note: Records and stats are through games played on September 13th.

First Place: Milwaukee Brewers (93-57)

Brice Turang (5.2 fWAR) Jacob Misiorowski (6.0 fWAR)

The Brewers won the race to be the first team to clinch a playoff spot over the weekend, and they’re now closing in on the NL Central title. They’re in a good position to finish with the best record in all of baseball as well.

They have an obvious absolute star in Misiorowski, but the most remarkable thing about the Brewers is that they’re just generally solid at almost every spot. Only one of their hitters with over 400 plate appearances has a wRC+ below the 100 average, and that’s Christian Yelich, who’s still in the 90s. You could’ve said similar things about last year’s Brewers, and they ended up getting shoved aside by the Dodgers in the NLCS, so we shall see.

Second Place: Chicago Cubs (83-67, 10 GB)

Pete Crow-Armstrong (9.8 fWAR) Ben Brown (2.0 fWAR)

Going into Monday, the Cubs would have the third best record were they an AL team. Instead in the NL Central, they’re way off the pace of the division lead. As of now, the Cubs are safely in the NL playoffs, but not so safe that they can rest on their laurels. They lost five of their last seven games going into Monday, so they can’t afford to let that skid continue.

As a team, the Cubs are incredibly reliant on their hitting and defense, while pitching has been a massive struggle for them. The two facets of the team are on such opposite poles that they’re going to go down as one of the most unbalanced teams of all time. They have the possible NL MVP in Crow-Armstrong, but can he and the rest of the lineup overcome that pitching? It’ll be fascinating to see play out.

Third Place: Pittsburgh Pirates (75-75, 18 GB)

Brandon Lowe (4.1 fWAR) Paul Skenes (4.8 fWAR)

It was wild to realize when putting together this post that the Pirates are basically in need of a miracle run to get into the playoffs in the NL, but they would be a game out of contention with that record in the AL.

It’s probably too late for Pittsburgh to rally and make the playoffs, but there are some things they can take away from this season. They’ve gotten some good seasons out of some of their young, up and coming players. One of those players is Skenes, who has only been merely “good” instead of “Cy Young Award great.” It’s somewhat worrying that he’s taken a step back, but if the Pirates figure that out, they could be a team that is intriguing next year.

Fourth Place: St. Louis Cardinals (74-76, 19 GB)

JJ Weatherholt (4.4 fWAR) Andre Pallante and Kyle Leahy (2.6 fWAR)

You can copy and paste some of what was said above about the Pirates and apply that to the Cardinals. Seven different St. Louis hitters aged 27 or younger have put up above average OPS+es on the season. Pallante and Michael McGreevy are both younger pitchers who’ve had pretty good years. They’re also gone nowhere in the standings, really.

Fifth Place: Cincinnati Reds (70-79, 22.5 GB)

Elly De La Cruz (5.7 fWAR) Chase Burns (4.4 fWAR)

The good news for the Reds is that Burns looks like a possible stud worthy of the No. 2 overall pick that he was in 24. More good news is that De La Cruz remains an absolute freak of nature and a genuine star. Not a ton else has gone right for Cincinnati, though. Their 22.5-game deficit in the division is the most of anyone in the league besides the Rockies and Giants in the NL West, both of whom are very bad.

items.title: MLB Mid-September Check-in: NL East
items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
Every day, Pinstripe Alley offers updates on what the ’ top American League opponents are up to through the . The AL East is well-trodden ground there, but with the season’s final month halfway over, we’re going to take a peek around MLB as a whole and check in with each of the other five divisions. Who’s surprising? Who’s underwhelming? Who’s simply mediocre at the moment? Read on and find out.

(Note: Records and standings are up to date through games played on Sunday, September 13th.)

First Place: Atlanta Braves (88-62)

Michael Harris II (4.0 fWAR)

Chris Sale (5.7 fWAR)

Believe it or not, the Atlanta Braves have had a below-average offense statistically so far in 2026, despite boasting elite names like Ronald Acuña Jr., Matt Olson, Michael Harris II, and Drake Baldwin. They rank 19th in wRC+ with a 98 mark.

The pitching has done the heavy lifting despite dealing with lots of injuries from the start. Right now, talented hurlers like Spencer Schwellenbach, Spencer Strider, Bryce Elder, and Robert Suárez are on the injured list, yet the team is fourth in MLB with a 3.59 ERA.

With a 3.41 ERA, the Braves’ bullpen is the best in the National League. It’s led by closer Raisel Iglesias (2.78 ERA), Didier Fuentes (2.27 ERA, 31.5 K%), Dylan Lee (3.09 ERA), and other unheralded heroes like Dylan Dodd, Víctor Mederos, Ray Kerr, and Brent Suter. The addition of Tyler Mahle (1.25 ERA in seven starts as a Brave) at the deadline was just what the doctor ordered, and Chris Sale (2.18 ERA) has been as good as ever.

Harris’ all-around game sets the tone, and Acuña’s power-speed prowess (17 HR, 20 SB in 97 G) elevates the team’s ceiling. Having Matt Olson picking up the power pace with 39 homers after two straight campaigns with 29 also helps, of course. The Braves, as their record indicates, are very hard to beat. Suárez returning from injury soon could make them even tougher.

Second Place: Philadelphia Phillies (83-67)

Bryce Harper (3.5 fWAR)

Christopher Sánchez (5.8 fWAR)

Bryce Harper refuses to decline and is sporting a cool 140 wRC+ with 28 home runs this year. He and Kyle Schwarber, who has 44 homers and owns a 132 wRC+, are virtually the Phillies’ offense, though: the unit has put up the fourth-worst wRC+ in baseball with a 92 mark. Trea Turner (83 wRC+) has had a rough season, and the same can be said about JT Realmuto (78 wRC+), Alec Bohm (89 wRC+), Luis Arraez (80 wRC+), and Justin Crawford (82 wRC+). Runs are hard to come by in Philadelphia.

Christopher Sánchez (2.79 ERA), Jesús Luzardo (2.87 ERA), and Zack Wheeler (3.14 ERA) are a formidable rotation trio, but Aaron Nola has been inconsistent, and there are now questions about the health of Luzardo’s shoulder.

Despite solid seasons from Jhoan Durán, Tim Mayza, and Jonathan Bowlan, the bullpen is more ‘meh’ than ‘great’. This team will go as far as the rotation takes it, although a rebound from some of their struggling hitters would certainly help matters. The Phillies are fighting with the Chicago Cubs for the top Wild Card spot in the senior circuit. Unless the offense improves, however, it’s hard to see them making much noise in October.

Third Place: Miami Marlins (74-76)

Otto López (5.4 fWAR)

Sandy Alcántara (3.1 fWAR)

The Marlins are 7.5 games behind the final Wild Card spot, so they aren’t really contending. After their disastrous 2024 and decent 2025, however, 2026 has been about finding potentially useful long-term pieces. And they have had some success.

As expected, Otto López’s stats have considerably diminished in the second half (79 wRC+, 1 HR, 13 SB) after a really strong performance before the break (137 wRC+, 9 HR, 17 SB). Still, a 10-homer, 30-steal season with a 116 wRC+ and 5.4 fWAR is nothing to sneeze at.

The Marlins’ offense, a perfectly average unit that ranks 14th in baseball, has some interesting hitters. With the exception of Joe Mack and Jakob Marsee, every starter boasts an above-average wRC+: Javier Sanoja, Xavier Edwards, Heriberto Hernández, Griffin Conine, Kyle Stowers, Esteury Ruiz, and López.

Before going down with a neck strain in July, Max Meyer (2.68 ERA in 20 starts) showed enough to be considered a frontline guy and a building block. Alcántara has been steady, and Eury Pérez had a huge summer before hitting a wall in September.

Overall, the Marlins have a solid core and a top-ten farm that includes injured pitching prospects Thomas White and Robby Snelling. If they play their cards right, they might make some noise next year.

Fourth Place: Washington Nationals (70-81)

James Wood (4.1 fWAR)

Cade Cavalli (3.6 fWAR)

Speaking of making noise, the Nationals’ offense can certainly score some runs. The group is fifth in MLB and fourth in the National League with a 104 wRC+, and ranks fourth in homers with 198. Of course, having James Wood (30 HR, 21 SB, 147 wRC+) and CJ Abrams (30 HR, 29 SB, 125 wRC+) certainly helps matters. These two will be a problem for MLB pitching staffs for a long time.

Dylan Crews’ development has stalled, and they don’t have Curtis Mead and Luis García Jr. anymore, but there’s a lot of talent in Washington’s offense besides the two aforementioned stars. Daylen Lile (20 HR, 15 SB) and Keibert Ruiz (113 wRC+) have had solid offensive seasons, and Brady House has potential. Former Yankees prospect Andrés Chaparro has been excellent against both lefties and righties.

Pitching, however, is a problem. Washington has the worst staff in the National League and the second-worst in the majors with a 5.14 ERA. Cade Cavalli (3.12 ERA) has had a breakout campaign, and Andrew Álvarez has been solid. There’s not much else beyond that, although adding the injured Connelly Early was a nice coup. The Nationals, with a solid core and a top-ten farm, are at the very least interesting again.

Fifth Place: New York Mets (69-80)

Carson Benge (3.3 fWAR)

Nolan McLean (3.1 fWAR)

The season in Queens has been a disaster, but it at least gave them a strong platform to develop Carson Benge and he’s looking like a budding star. The rookie outfielder is slashing a cool .271/.334/.411 with a 109 wRC+, 17 home runs and 22 steals after a brutal start. Juan Soto has survived two injured list stints to post a 147 wRC+ and 25 round-trippers, and Francisco Lindor reached 20 dingers with a solid 111 after having to deal with hamate bone surgery.

A.J. Ewing emerged as another potential building block in the outfield, although it remains to be seen if he’s a starter or more of a fourth outfielder. Brett Baty, who was brutal for most of the first half, is closing the season strong with a 125 wRC+ after the break and a 236 mark in September so far.

Despite trading away Clay Holmes, Freddy Peralta, and lots of relievers at the deadline, the Mets have a top-ten ERA in the second half, at 3.38. Zach Thornton and Nate Lavender have been amazing stories in the rotation and bullpen, respectively, and Nolan McLean and Christian Scott are excellent building blocks.

With a few interesting young pieces, two superstars, and lots of money to spend, the Mets could be dangerous in 2027, if there’s baseball. The 2026 campaign, however, was a huge disappointment.

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Slow Joe Doyle
items.author: Jonathan Farrar
items.content:
Before he was known as Slow Joe, Judd Bruce Doyle was a right-handed pitcher growing up in the middle of Kansas. Like most of the time, his love of baseball was not born in an organized league, but in the school lot and in local games in his community featuring players of all ages.

September 15, 1881 (Clay Center, KS) November 21, 1947 (Tannersville, NY) 1906-1910

Born before the turn of the century, Doyle was small even by the standards of the time. He was reported by most accounts at 5-foot-8 and 150 pounds. However, growing up working on the family farm made Doyle what many call country strong or stout. Despite having some strength behind his small frame, Doyle relied on changing pace and his arm slots to keep hitters off balance, much like former Yankee folk hero Nestor Cortes. Doyle and his mix of overhand and submarine deliveries tossed a drop ball, rise ball, changeup, and the legendary spitball.

Doyle’s professional baseball journey started right after he graduated from Clay Center High School in 1901. This kicked off a five-year run through the amateur ranks. In 1902, Doyle suited up for the Fort Worth Panthers and the New Orleans Pelicans. Then, in 1903, Doyle joined the Baton Rouge Red Sticks in the Cotton States League. In his first season in Baton Rouge, Doyle went 16-9 and helped the team win the league championship. He started the 1904 season back in a Red Sticks jersey, but would finish that season and play the 1905 season for the Wheeling Stogies.

After playing well for the Stogies, Doyle finally landed the coveted contract with a professional team when his rights were sold to the New York Highlanders in August of 1905. Slow Joe burst onto the scene a few days later, making his debut on August 25, 1906. In his first start, Doyle threw a six-hit shutout against the Cleveland Naps. He followed that up with another shutout against the Washington Senators in his second game. The rookie appeared in nine games total, tossing 45.1 innings with a 2-1 record and 2.38 ERA.

Following the hot start to his career, Doyle came into the 1907 season expecting to be a big part of the Highlanders rotation. Doyle appeared in 29 games, making 23 starts. This led to what would stand as his career-high 193.2 innings with an impressive 2.65 ERA and an 11-11 record. Doyle led the Highlanders with 15 complete games and 94 strikeouts. It was also during this run that his reputation for slow playing really took hold. The Washington Times referred to Doyle as the Human Snail due to his long stretches between pitches.

In 1908, Doyle’s third season, Slow Joe was officially the name adopted and used by the press as an unofficial, official name. Doyle’s arm did not handle the large workload from the year before well, and he was limited to 12 games, only four starts, and only 48 innings. Despite being effective when he pitched, the lack of availability started to be the story.

Doyle asked for extra days of rest between starts in 1909, and it led to a rebound. He pitched in 17 games, making 15 starts, tossing 125.2 innings, and going 8-6 on the year. Still just 27 years old, Doyle’s arm simply could not handle the workload of a normal pitcher of the time.

The Highlanders had Doyle on their roster to start the 1910 season but ended up cutting him halfway through the year. The Cincinnati Reds signed Doyle, and he pitched the final part of the season for them. After making five relief appearances for the Reds, Doyle’s major league career was over at just 28 years old after the 1910 season.

Beyond his memorable nickname, Slow Joe Doyle holds a legendary status among modern sports collectors due to one of the rarest and most valuable printing blunders in baseball history: the 1910 T206 “Slow Joe” Doyle error card. During the production of the iconic tobacco card set, the American Lithographic Company accidentally designated Doyle as playing for “Nat’l” rather than “Amer” in his New York uniform. After catching the mistake, the printers pulled the printing plate, scrapped off the “Nat’l” letters, slapped the plate back into the machine, and continued printing. Today, fewer than a dozen authentic copies are known to exist, making it more rare than the famed Honus Wagner T206 card.

Happy birthday, Slow Joe!

items.title: Yankees Rivalry Roundup: Blue Jays loss leads to Yanks’ playoff clinch
items.author: Andrew Mearns
items.content:
The Yankees were the only member of the top trio of American League teams playing on Monday, with both the Rays and Red Sox off inadvance of series against the A’s and Rangers, respectively. The AL West-leading [read: .500] Astros were also sidelined. So yeah, if the 2026 Yankees are the gold standard, then you know it’s a dreary night of action. Thankfully, they took care of their own business after a slow start by dropping a six-spot in the eighth inning on their ol’ Twins pals in the eighth inning to win on Clinching Day.

As it turned out though, the Yankees had already punched their 61st ticket to the postseason! Here’s what the teams that active were up to on Monday night.

Chicago White Sox (77-73) 7, Cleveland Guardians (76-75) 3

Separated by a half-game before first pitch, the White Sox and Guardians squared off in Cleveland to begin a three-game set that could decide both the AL Central and—believe it or not with these records—a first-round bye. It was a scoreless duel through five, with Guardos ace Gavin Williams and the opener/bulk guy combo of Sean Newcomb and Sean Burke putting goose eggs on the board. Williams returned to the mound in the sixth, looking for a couple more punchouts to tie and surpass both Dylan Cease and Jacob Misiorowski (236) for the MLB lead. Instead, was the one who got punc—OK you get it.

It started innocently enough with an infield hit by Andrew Benintendi. Then came one of the most remarkable at-bats of the entire season, as Tristan Peters worked Williams for 18 pitches before taking a walk. It was the longest at-bat (well, plate appearance I suppose) since a 19-pitch battle by Matt Wieters for the 2020 Cardinals (sure?).

Peters had worked Williams’ pitch count up to 113 by that point, so he was done for the night. Tim Herrin replaced him, and he honestly did his job by getting a double-play ball to first baseman Nathaniel Lowe. But Lowe’s throw to second caromed off Peters’ helmet and scored Benintendi for the first run of the game.

From there, the wheels came off. Chase Meidroth singled in a second, Randal Grichuk got a knock to load the bases, Kyle Teel doubled in a pair, and after Daniel Espino replaced Herrin, Miguel Vargas dropped the hammer with a two-run bomb:

Burke gave one back in the home half and David Fry at least briefly woke up the home crowd with a two-run homer with two down in the ninth, but this never felt close after that one inning. Final score: 7-3, Chicago, and a 1.5-game lead in the AL Central.

Toronto Blue Jays (75-76) 5, Detroit Tigers (71-79) 6: Most Yankees fans’ eyes were directed at this game though, as either a Jays loss or Yankees win would punch the Bombers’ ticket to the postseason. They got both! The Jays’ loss came a little less than half an hour before New York beat Minnesota, so the Yanks got to feel good in the dugout for just a bit before they celebrated on the field.

For awhile, it looked like the wait would continue until at least tomorrow, as the Yanks trailed the Twins 2-1 through seven while the Jays rallied against the Tigers. Detroit had taken a 4-2 lead in the seventh with José Soriano set his no-hit bid ablaze, as Max Clark and Spencer Torkelson both doubled to get the Tigers ahead. But a three-run blast by Kazuma Okamoto brought the Jays back in front, 5-4. A year ago, this probably would’ve been a propeller of sorts; however, these Jays are not the same, and neither is weary Louie Varland. A pair of hits off Joe Mantiply set up the game-tying Tigers attack in the eighth on a flare to left by Brett Callahan against Varland, and a leadoff walk put Varland in position to fumble the ball away as the go-ahead run crossed home.

After his own leadoff walk, Kenley Jansen struck out Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and got Alejandro Kirk to bounce into a game-ending double play for his 496th career save. The Jays still trail the Guardians by a game in the AL Wild Card with the Rangers one win behind them.

Baltimore Orioles (73-78) 2, New York Mets (69-81) 1: The O’s are just barely alive in this Wild Card conversation as well, but they got the win they needed to get to three games back; they’ll need many more this week! This one was all about Pete Alonso’s long-awaited return to Queens, and the Mets fans showered him with affection on a night in which they were (appropriately) eliminated. Alonso took an oh-fer, but Gunnar Henderson broke a 1-1 tie in the eighth with a solo shot and Rico Garcia held on to close it out.

items.title: Yankees At-Bat(s) of the Week: Anthony Volpe (9/10)
items.author: Peter Brody
items.content:
I’m sure Anthony Volpe wanted to make a statement in his first game back from his demotion to Triple-A on August 4th, but I bet even he couldn’t have dreamt of the impact he would author. In his first MLB action in over a month, Volpe arrived in the Bronx sporting new swing mechanics and the results were immediate, the much-maligned infielder going 3-for-4 with a grand slam and a career-high five RBI. It’s his first and last ABs from that game that I would like to highlight today.

We first join Volpe with no outs in the bottom of the second last Thursday against the Rockies. The Yankees need to complete the sweep and have created a promising opportunity early with Ryan McMahon singling and Austin Wells drawing a walk to open the frame. They already lead, 2-1, courtesy of a Luis García Jr. two-run blast in the first, but after Max Fried surrendered a solo shot to Kyle Karros in the second, it became imperative that the Yankees take advantage of this scoring chance given the uncertainty of how many innings they’ll get from their starter recently back from injury.

Ryan Feltner starts Volpe with a first pitch sinker low hoping for an early double play ball.

Really excellent take here from Volpe, this sinker looking like a strike middle-down until about the last ten feet before home. I almost wonder if he was hunting something in a different zone the way the bat never left his shoulder on such a borderline pitch.

Feltner executed that sinker pretty much how he intended, so despite not getting the result he wanted, there is no need for him to deviate course.

Volpe follows up that excellent take with a positively head-scratching one. This sinker looks like a strike right down the middle the moment it leaves Feltner’s hand and never leaves the zone, yet Volpe watches it all the way into the catcher’s glove for strike one.

Ok, now I officially have no idea what Volpe is looking for. That’s two straight meatball sinkers from Feltner. The first he showed zero interest in offering at. This sinker is as center-cut as they come, yet all Volpe can do is fire a late emergency hack as if he is sitting on something else and gets surprised that this pitch is in a hittable location. This is a pitch he should be crushing but instead he’s swinging as if to fight it off foul to stay alive in a 1-1 count.

At this point I just assumed this AB would end the way a lot of two-strike counts against Volpe end — a strikeout swinging on a breaking ball out of the zone. So far it’s been same old, same old from Volpe, failing to take advantage of mistake pitches early in the count and thus needlessly fall behind, which around these circles we know as a non-competitive AB. Feltner has been gifted an opportunity for a strikeout and his first pitch selection to get it is the changeup.

Feltner misses wildly with this changeup, sailing it way up and in when he meant to locate it down below the zone. A completely non-competitive pitch and an automatic take from Volpe.

Feltner immediately shelves the changeup after such a wayward misfire and switches to the secondary that has given Volpe fits his whole big league career — the low and away slider.

Wow, this was… an impressively disciplined take from Volpe. This pitch looks exactly like the two in-zone sinkers that Volpe failed to punish earlier in the AB before taking a sharp left turn about halfway to the plate. You can tell that Volpe recognized the pitch pretty soon out of Feltner’s had based on the minimal flinch as he takes it for ball three.

Volpe has done well to work the count full after falling behind, 1-2. Feltner does not want to walk the bases loaded with no outs and the top of the order coming up, so he is somewhat forced into throwing sinkers in the zone again in the hope of inducing a double play ball.

This one lands in almost the same spot as the one Volpe took for strike one. This time he does elect to swing, but it’s not a particularly good swing. His whole front side flies open, causing the bat head to come around and over the top of the baseball, and all he can do is ground it foul to the pull side.

With a swing like that, Feltner must feel confident he can get Volpe to roll over a grounder if he can command his sinker lower than the last three he threw.

Instead, this sinker sails up and in just like the one changeup Feltner threw earlier. Volpe is a little unlucky that the pitch hit his bat on the check swing, otherwise he would have drawn the walk to load the bases.

After showing Volpe four fastballs with sinking movement in this AB, Feltner finally breaks out the four-seamer hoping that a straight flying heater will stay above Volpe’s barrel for a strikeout.

Volpe is sitting dead red, which is how he is able to make solid contact with this 95 mph four-seamer bearing in on his hands. The early swing allows him to get the bat head out and pull a sharp grounder through the hole on the left side for an RBI single to restore the Yankees’ two-run cushion.

We have to fast-forward to the seventh for the real fireworks. An RBI triple by Jake McCarthy in the top-half briefly made it 4-2, but a Cody Bellinger leadoff double, Jasson Domínguez walk, and Spencer Jones two-run single provided a cushion at 6-2. McMahon and Wells then drew a pair of two-out walks to load the bases for Volpe, who steps to the plate with the confidence of a pair of singles already to his name.

Unlike Feltner, Jimmy Herget looks to pitch Volpe backwards, starting with breaking balls away to slow down his bat and get him leaning out over the plate to in theory set up a heater inside later in the count.

This is a perfect slider from Herget, dotted right on the corner low and away. Even though it lands for a called strike, it’s still a good take from Volpe. Had he swung, at best you’re looking at a whiff and more likely an inning ending grounder.

Having earned the strike looking with that slider, Herget shows some impressive sequencing by throwing a sweeper out of the same slot — it should look like the slider Volpe just saw only this time with a foot-and-a-half more lateral movement away from the batter.

This is the best take from Volpe all game and maybe all season. This sweeper comes down the exact same tunnel as the slider that was just called a strike on the outside edge. You would expect most hitters to chase this pitch — they are forced to protect that outside edge now that the pitcher has established his breaking ball for a called strike in that quadrant. Just like the close slider he took for a ball just off the plate away from Feltner, Volpe must have gotten a good read on the spin of this pitch to layoff with hardly a flinch.

Despite not getting the chase, Herget sticks with his plan of soft away, hard in. He looks to bear a sinker in on Volpe’s hands for some weak contact.

Instead, he leaves this 91 mph sinker middle-middle, and unlike in the first AB we covered, Volpe doesn’t miss it. Volpe stays inside the baseball and drives it to the opposite field, short porching Herget for a grand slam. The swing is a thing of beauty, Volpe precise with his barrel to the baseball while showing an impressive amount of power despite taking an opposite-field approach.

The Yankees ended up routing the Rockies, 10-3, and Volpe single-handedly drove in half those runs. During the game, we learned about several mechanical adjustment Volpe implemented in his month-plus at Triple-A.

I spot two major differences at the initiation of the load phase: higher hand positioning and a small step back with his back foot. Starting with the hand positioning, I feel that this helps prevent Volpe from casting his swing — you can see how before the demotion his front elbow straightens out well before contact whereas on the grand slam swing, that front elbow stays bent and tight to the body. When you straighten your front elbow too soon, your hands tend to drift away from the body, causing the bat head to lag and the swing to become long and loopy. This robs you of power, prevents you from going to the opposite field, and makes it almost impossible to catch up to the heater. Keeping the front elbow tucked leads to a shorter, more compact swing, allowing Volpe to stay inside the baseball to drive it with power the other way as the barrel rotates in sync with the torso.

The adjustment that has me really excited, however, is the step back. Paul O’Neill noticed it right away on the broadcast and could not offer enough praise for the adjustment. He explained the way that that step forces Volpe to keep his weight back, allowing him to stay behind the baseball which is critical for efficiently transferring all of the stored potential energy from trunk to arms to bat. The hallmark of Volpe’s struggles is when he bails on his front side, the front hip and shoulder flying open way too early. This causes Volpe to step in the bucket, or fall with his weight toward third base rather than stride toward the pitcher, which not only robs him of power but is the prime culprit for all those whiffs against breaking balls away as Volpe deprives himself of plate coverage. This new step back is a godsend. In forcing him to keep his weight back a tick longer and stride forward instead of open, Volpe’s barrel should remain in the hitting zone for far longer than when he’s cutting across the zone when stepping in the bucket, which is how he is able to to drive a slightly inside pitch out of the park the other way.

We’ve seen Volpe make mechanical adjustments in the past and then get hot for a few weeks. However, without fail he has let those past adjustments fall by the wayside and revert back to his old bad habits every single time. Hopefully, this time around these changes are here to stay.

items.title: The Yankees have found a way in 2026
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
The Yankees will officially be playing baseball in October after last night’s loss by Toronto, shortly followed by New York’s own win allowing for a more raucous celebration rather than a somber one. It has not come easily for them this year, as they’ve weathered more than their fair share of blows to key players and endured lengthy slumps from others, but the man who has stood at the helm all year coasted them through to the starting line once again.

I’m not one to subscribe to the notion that managers strongly impact the game positively or negatively, but Aaron Boone has been a lightning rod for criticism throughout his tenure in New York for a whole host of reasons out of his control on top of some that he does hold some influence over, so I think it’s only fair to give him some credit for what has been an incredibly difficult season to navigate. Losing Aaron Judge to start June and not getting him back until September was a severe blow to the team, as it would’ve been at any point over the last near decade, and the offense withered without him for a long while. Unlike when he went down in 2023, however, this year’s Yankees didn’t collapse with the captain out of commission, and though they tried their hardest to make the games frustrating they managed to walk the tightrope convincingly enough to stay afloat in the standings.

You could certainly credit a large portion of that success to a stronger and deeper rotation this season compared to when they were rolling out Gerrit Cole and a bunch of bodies and I’d agree, but there’s been turmoil there too as injuries continually prevented the Yankees from lining up their five best starters in a given turn through the order. On top of that, the pitching staff as a whole was a little suspect with a bullpen that many questioned at the start of the year — for good reason as it turned out. David Bednar was unquestioned as the closer, though he struggled out of the gate, but the bridge to Bednar was rickety and swinging on frayed rope at the start of the year. Fernando Cruz was a solid option who earned some late-inning appearances, but unfortunately an elbow injury has put his season (and perhaps Yankees career) in jeopardy. Camilo Doval was the initial setup man, but he turned out to be a bust in pinstripes and there were only question marks surrounding the rest of the relief corps.

The emergence of Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick forming the big three at the back of the ‘pen quite possibly is the biggest reason that this team is leading the Wild Card standings with a shot at the division still, their lock-down performances holding slim lead after slim lead and putting out fires whenever called upon having bailed out an offense that looked downright putrid for weeks. Boone has rarely leaned so heavily on a pair of arms before, but he’s fitted the two into the Scott Proctor mold and reaped the rewards for doing so while seemingly keeping them fresh enough as we enter the final stretch of the regular season.

The bullpen management has been his biggest success, but Boone and the front office have pushed the right buttons in a number of areas. The team was getting nothing out of the catcher position offensively in the first half of the year, but they surprised many by not acquiring a catcher at the Trade Deadline and instead affirming their faith in Austin Wells, who shepherded the pitchers well enough but had been absolutely dreadful with the bat. He turned around and gave them a respectable July before hitting above-average in August, and though he’s gone through another slump in September he’s still become more than respectable in the lineup again. Wells is far from the only regular they’ve been rewarded for believing in — Jazz Chisholm Jr. endured a topsy-turvy season that drew plenty of criticism after he put a goal of 50 home runs and 50 steals on his shoulders in spring. The homers never came close as he hit only six through the first two months, but Jazz has gotten close on the basepaths with 40 stolen bags this year. The option of flipping Chisholm ahead of his impending free agency was floated in trade rumors but never emerged, and instead he’s turned in a season that will end up coming close to his previous two years by fWAR.

The only real shakeup that Brian Cashman made to this roster came at the deadline, where the team traded for Luis García Jr. and Heliot Ramos — a pair of platoon bats, though García was the big get having led the National League in slugging when he was moved and has played accordingly since. From within they called up George Lombard Jr. and sent Anthony Volpe down to Triple-A to work on his maligned offensive capabilities while also considering new positions. Both moves paid dividends, with Lombard providing a spark and an injection of youth to the lineup while Volpe got a hero’s return on Thursday when he hit a grand slam against the Rockies and received a curtain call from the fans. I can’t imagine that when Volpe was demoted he was ever significantly in the team’s immediate plans for the rest of the year, but injuries again pressed them and their choice to finally allow Volpe the space to work on his craft has paid off with him sliding into second base in Chisholm’s absence.

There’s a dozen points where this season could’ve gone up in flames for the Yankees, but here they stand in the middle of September with a ticket to at least two guaranteed games of postseason baseball with the potential for more. The division is still within their grasp even if time is running out, and they simply can’t control how well the Rays have played. They can only handle their own business, and they’ve done a phenomenal job of doing just that this year.

items.title: Yankees prospects: Week 25 minor league recap
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
We’ve reached the final stretch, folks. One week from today, we could be completely done with minor league baseball. Hudson Valley concluded a week ago, Somerset concluded on Sunday, Tampa will conclude on Wednesday at the latest, and Scranton will need a huge week to see their season go past this coming Sunday.

As we begin to wind down the minor league recaps, we bid adieu to the 2026 Somerset Patriots while checking in on the RailRiders’ playoff push and Tampa’s journey to an FSL championship.

Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders

38-30 (75-66), 2 GB in the International League East after a 2-4 week against the Rochester Red Wings (Nationals)

+55 (+58)

Home vs. Jacksonville Jumbo Shrimp (Marlins)

That’s a back-breaking week for the RailRiders’ playoff hopes. They entered the week in a dead draw with Rochester, so whoever won this series was going to have the definitive advantage heading into the final week. Almost every game could’ve gone both ways, but they’re going to really be hurting over Saturday and Sunday, blowing a 6-0 lead in the former and coming up short on a late rally in the latter. They’ll now need to pick up three games in the last week to make the playoffs.

It was a pretty meh week for the offense, with the exception of some late-week heroics by Oswaldo Cabrera (multi-homer game on Sunday) and Marco Luciano (homered in consecutive games). We also saw Duke Ellis surpass 50 stolen bases, continuing a remarkable streak of baserunning excellence. It truly is something to behold how many guys down here have major league experience and prior notoriety, and that’s not even counting Mitch Garver, who continues to be in limbo after neither the Yankees nor anyone else wanted to add him to their active roster before the September 1st deadline. Not sure what’s going on there.

As for the rotation, Alexander Cornielle drew double duty and continued his strong stretch on Monday before struggling on Sunday. Elmer Rodríguez tossed four shutout innings before getting blown up in the fifth on Friday, while Kyle Carr and Xavier Rivas continued to do their piggyback system, with the latter picking up his first Triple-A win with five solid innings. Once again, Brendan Beck was the standardbearer of the week, tossing 5.1 shutout innings to continue one of the best years by a minor league starter this season. Funny enough, the Yankees have the only two starters with a sub-3 ERA and 100 innings at the level: him and Elmer.

As you might expect from a bad week, the bullpen didn’t do its job. Eric Reyzelman and Chris Kean both tossed two scoreless innings, but the veterans weren’t as sharp, namely Justin Topa, Yerry de los Santos, and Eli Morgan.

37-32 (74-64), 3.5 GB in the Eastern League Northeast after a 4-2 week against the Hartford Yard Goats (Rockies)

+9 (+45)

Somerset’s season came to an end this week after going 4-2 against Hartford. They played too mediocre over the last several weeks to make a serious playoff push, and wound up playing out the string this week with a group that looked a helluva lot different than the offensive juggernaut they had on Opening Day.

We saw great finishes to the season by Core Jackson and Roderick Arias, two guys who’ve had chaotic seasons. Jackson had three different IL stints, while Arias had a nightmarish start before completely saving his prospect stock with an incredible finish. The two constants at this level all season were Jace Avina and Coby Morales. The former was incredible through the end of July but had a tough end to the season. Morales was incredibly consistent from start to finish as a 20/20 bat, having found a power stroke that eluded him early in his pro career.

On the pitching side, it’s a season of disappointment. Ben Hess only pitched 56.2 innings before going on the injured list; Cade Smith had a tumultuous and inconsistent season; and the rotation spent much of the last several weeks being heavily reliant on bullpen games. Two late call-ups really opened some eyes, though. Bryce Cunningham finished strong in what felt like a lost season for a while, and Rory Fox capped his first pro season with 7.2 scoreless innings this past week and a 3.97 ERA across 47.2 innings post-promotion.

Ultimately, there’s a bunch of players here who we could see in Scranton next year, but also a handful I’d expect to start next year in Somerset, namely Arias, Jackson, Cunningham, and Fox. We’ll see if they’re joined by some aggressive promotions lower on the farm.

75-48, swept Clearwater in FSL Division Series. Down 1-0 to Jupiter in FSL Championship Series

Games 2 and 3 of FSL Championship Series vs. Jupiter Hammerheads (Marlins)

Tampa played just three games this week, breezing past Clearwater in a two-game sweep to get to the FSL Championship Series. They lost Game 1 of that series, 9-1, in a game that was blown open in the ninth via a seven spot. They’ll have to win the next two, which doesn’t seem impossible for the hottest team in Single-A, which swept Jupiter in a five-game series at the end of August.

Game 1 against Clearwater was a sleepy 2-0 win. Both runs were scored off a rehabbing Nestor Cortes, with the RBI knocks coming from Yostin Pena (2-3, RBI, BB, R, SB) and Paul Gutierrez-Contreras II (1-3, RBI, 2B). J.T. Etheridge tossed five shutout innings to continue an incredible last few weeks, while being backed up by sharp relief from Antonio Gomez, Jose Ledesma, and Matthew Tippie.

Game 2 was higher scoring, but also more tense. Gutierrez-Contreras blasted a fourth-inning homer, but the team trailed 3-2 after seven. Hoping to finish things off quickly, Pena ripped an RBI double off the wall in center field before Wilberson De Pena crushed a go-ahead home run. Add a two-run single by Tyce Armstrong, and they had what they needed to win, even with Tippie’s ninth-inning struggles. Tyler Boudreau returned after taking a nasty comebacker last week and struck out nine in five innings, but had to settle for a no-decision in a 7-5 win to secure the sweep.

In Game 1 of the FSL Championship Series on Sunday, this dynamic offense was completely silenced aside from a Luis Escudero home run in the eighth inning. Justin West tossed five shutout innings to continue his strong second half by him, but the bullpen allowed nine runs in the final few innings. Yeesh.

items.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 9/15/26
items.author: Madison Pavich
items.content:
It wasn’t looking pretty for seven innings, but the Yankees finally erupted in the eighth to put away the Twins and secure the series opener. With the Blue Jays losing earlier in the night, the Yanks officially clinched a playoff spot and the celebration was on once their game was over. With the Rays and Red Sox inactive, it was also a day to gain a half-game in the standings, and they’ll need to keep moving up ahead of their matchup with the former if they want a shot at the division still.

Today on the site, I’ll start things off with a look at how Aaron Boone and company managed to squeeze out wins despite the valleys they went through. Michael’s up next with the weekly minor league recap, Andrew has the Rivalry Roundup featuring the loss that officially sent the Yankees into October, and Jonathan highlights Slow Joe Doyle’s days with the Highlanders on his birthday. Later in the day we’ve got our three remaining division check-ins, Andres scoping out the NL East, Matt scouting the NL Central, and Estevao combing through the NL West.

New York Yankees at Minnesota Twins

TV: YES Network, Twins.tv

Venue: Target Field, Minneapolis, MN

1. Will we get to see Max Fried get deep into his pitch count tonight, or will the team keep him in this 75-80 pitch range?

2. Now that Aaron Judge has his first home run since coming off the IL, how many more do you think he’ll run into to close out the year?
